prompts.research:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Current Employment Statistics (CES)
Description: The Current Employment Statistics (CES) program is a monthly survey conducted by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The survey provides employment, hours, and earnings estimates based on payroll records of business establishments.
URL: https://bls.gov/ces

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Transmission of material in this news release is embargoed until                       USDL-26-1549
8:30 a.m. (ET) Friday, October 2, 2026

Technical information:
 Household data:      (202) 691-6378  *  cpsinfo@bls.gov  *  www.bls.gov/cps
 Establishment data:  (202) 691-6555  *  cesinfo@bls.gov  *  www.bls.gov/ces

Media contact:        (202) 691-5902  *  PressOffice@bls.gov


                            THE EMPLOYMENT SITUATION - SEPTEMBER 2026


Both nonfarm payroll employment (+29,000) and the unemployment rate (4.2 percent) changed little in 
September, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment in all major industries 
changed little over the month.

This news release presents statistics from two monthly surveys. The household survey measures labor 
force status, including unemployment, by demographic characteristics. The establishment survey 
measures nonfarm employment, hours, and earnings by industry. For more information about the 
concepts and statistical methodology used in these two surveys, see the Technical Note.

Household Survey Data

Both the unemployment rate, at 4.2 percent, and the number of unemployed people, at 7.1 million, 
changed little in September. The unemployment rate has remained in a narrow range of 4.1 percent to 
4.3 percent since March. (See table A-1.)

Among the major worker groups, the unemployment rate for people who are Black (7.0 percent)
increased in September. The jobless rates for adult men (3.9 percent), adult women (3.6 percent), 
teenagers (14.5 percent), and people who are White (3.6 percent), Asian (2.9 percent), or Hispanic 
(4.7 percent) showed little change over the month. (See tables A-1, A-2, and A-3.)

The number of long-term unemployed (those jobless for 27 weeks or more) was essentially unchanged 
at 1.9 million in September. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.1 percent of all unemployed 
people. (See table A-12.)

Both the labor force participation rate, at 61.8 percent, and the employment-population ratio, at 
59.2 percent, changed little in September. These measures showed little net change since January. 
(See table A-1.)

The number of people employed part time for economic reasons changed little at 4.5 million in 
September. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time 
because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs. (See table A-8.)

In September, the number of people not in the labor force who currently want a job changed little 
at 5.8 million. These individuals were not counted as unemployed because they were not actively 
looking for work during the 4 weeks preceding the survey or were unavailable to take a job. (See 
table A-1.)

Among those not in the labor force who wanted a job, the number of people marginally attached to 
the labor force decreased by 236,000 to 1.5 million in September. These individuals wanted and were 
available for work and had looked for a job sometime in the prior 12 months but had not looked for 
work in the 4 weeks preceding the survey. The number of discouraged workers, a subset of the 
marginally attached who believed that no jobs were available for them, changed little over the 
month at 414,000. (See Summary table A.)

Establishment Survey Data

Total nonfarm payroll employment changed little in September (+29,000), following an average 
monthly gain of 45,000 over the prior 12 months. Employment in all major industries changed little 
over the month. (See table B-1.)

Health care employment continued its upward trend in September (+17,000), but at a slower pace than 
the average monthly gain over the prior 12 months (+33,000). In September, employment continued to 
trend up in ambulatory health care services (+13,000) and in hospitals (+12,000), while nursing and 
residential care facilities lost jobs (-9,000).

Employment in construction changed little in September (+11,000). The industry had added an average 
of 10,000 jobs per month over the prior 12 months. In September, employment in nonresidential 
specialty trade contractors continued to trend up (+12,000).

Manufacturing employment was little changed in September (+9,000) but is up by 72,000 since a 
recent low in December 2025. Over the month, employment increased in plastics and rubber products
manufacturing (+5,000) and in machinery manufacturing (+5,000).

In September, financial activities employment was little changed (-7,000

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Current Employment Statistics (CES)
Description: The Current Employment Statistics (CES) program is a monthly survey conducted by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The survey provides employment, hours, and earnings estimates based on payroll records of business establishments.
URL: https://bls.gov/ces

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the Current Employment Statistics program comprehensively. Let me start with several searches covering different aspects.Good foundation. Now let me research the legal authority, data access methods, and users of the data.I have solid coverage of legal authority and data access. Now let me research data users, benchmark revisions (including the notable 2025 revision), and confidentiality/statistical policy aspects.The search limit was reached, but I can still fetch pages directly to fill remaining gaps on confidentiality and reliability.I now have comprehensive coverage from primary sources (BLS Handbook of Methods, the U.S. Code, OMB's ICR record, BLS technical notes and news releases, and peer research from NBER). Here is the complete report.

---

# Research Report: Current Employment Statistics (CES)

## 1. Dataset Identification & Verification of Your Description

**Your description is accurate.** Verified against BLS's own program overview: *"The Current Employment Statistics (CES) program is a monthly survey conducted by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The survey provides employment, hours, and earnings estimates based on payroll records of business establishments."* — this is verbatim from BLS (bls.gov/web/empsit/cesprog.htm). The URL you provided (bls.gov/ces) resolves to the CES-National homepage at www.bls.gov/ces/.

One clarification worth knowing: "CES" actually covers **two closely related programs** that share the same sample and collection methods:

- **CES-National (CES-N)** — https://www.bls.gov/ces/ — national estimates of nonfarm employment, hours, and earnings by industry.
- **CES-State and Metro Area (CES-SA)** — https://www.bls.gov/sae/ — estimates for all 50 states, D.C., Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and ~400 metropolitan areas/divisions. (National estimates exclude Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands.)

Both are **federal–state cooperative programs**: the sample is collected largely by state workforce agencies (SWAs) under cooperative agreements, with BLS providing funding, sampling requirements, estimation guidelines, and national publication. This is one of the oldest continuous federal–state statistical partnerships in the U.S.

## 2. Publisher & Institutional Home

- **Publisher:** U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), an agency of the U.S. Department of Labor, under the direction of the Secretary of Labor.
- **Parent data ecosystem:** CES is one of the BLS employment/unemployment family of programs, alongside the Current Population Survey (CPS, the household survey), Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS), and Business Employment Dynamics (BDM).
- **Status as an economic indicator:** CES is designated a **Principal Federal Economic Indicator (PFEI)** under OMB Statistical Policy Directive 3. Per BLS's own Paperwork Reduction Act filing (OMB Control No. 1220-0011): *"CES estimates are among the most visible and widely-used Principal Federal Economic Indicators… The statistics are fundamental inputs in economic decision processes at all levels of government, private enterprise, and organized labor."* As a PFEI, it is subject to strict OMB rules on pre-release access, embargo, and release-date publication well in advance.

## 3. Legal Authority & Mandate

The program rests on a century-old statutory foundation (codified in Title 29 of the U.S. Code, Chapter 1, originally enacted as part of the 1913 act creating the Department of Labor, with the employment-statistics language added July 7, 1930):

- **29 U.S.C. § 1** — the general mandate of BLS: to *"acquire and diffuse among the people of the United States useful information on subjects connected with labor… the hours of labor, the earnings of laboring men and women…"*
- **29 U.S.C. § 2** — the specific monthly mandate: BLS must *"collect, collate, report, and publish at least once each month full and complete statistics of the volume of and changes in employment, as indicated by the number of persons employed, the total wages paid, and the total hours of employment"* in federal, state, and local government and across enumerated industries (manufacturing; mining; construction; agriculture/lumbering; transportation, communication and utilities; retail and wholesale trade; *"and such other industries as the Secretary of Labor may deem it in the public interest to include"*), nationally **and by state/Federal Reserve district and smaller geographic subdivisions**. This clause is the direct statutory ancestor of today's CES, including its state and metro products.
- **29 U.S.C. §§ 7–8 (subchapter II)** — authorizes special statistical studies on request (cost-reimbursable).

**Administrative/legal framework:**
- **Paperwork Reduction Act clearance:** OMB Control No. **1220-0011** (CES is one of the longest-standing ICRs; renewal packages are publicly visible on reginfo.gov and omb.report, which are excellent documentary evidence trails).
- **Confidentiality:** CES respondent data are protected as confidential statistical information under the **Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act (CIPSEA)**, as amended in 2018.
- **Participation is voluntary under federal law.** Notably, it is **mandatory under state law in California, New Mexico, Oregon, South Carolina, and Puerto Rico** (South Carolina's requirement applies only to firms with more than 20 employees) — legal citations appear on the state report forms.
- The federal–state structure operates via cooperative agreements authorized by § 2's provision that the Secretary may *"arrange with any Federal, State, or municipal bureau or other governmental agency for the collection of such statistics."*

## 4. History (1915–Present)

CES is **the oldest continuous federal employment statistics program**, and its history is unusually well documented (BLS maintains a CES History chapter in the Handbook of Methods and published a centennial retrospective series in the *Monthly Labor Review* in 2015–16). Key milestones:

- **1915 (October):** BLS begins collecting employment and payroll data for **four manufacturing industries** (boots and shoes, cotton goods, cotton finishing, hosiery and underwear). Predecessor state surveys existed in New York, New Jersey, and Massachusetts.
- **1916:** First federal–state cooperative agreement (New York); expansion to 13 industries, 574 establishments.
- **1923:** Expansion to 52 manufacturing industries, following recommendations of the **Committee on Employment Statistics commissioned by President Warren G. Harding** and increased congressional funding.
- **1929:** First nonmanufacturing industries (11) published, following American Statistical Association committee recommendations; sample reaches 34,000 establishments.
- **1931:** President Hoover's Advisory Committee on Employment Statistics recommends benchmarking to the Census of Manufactures and collecting hours data.
- **1932:** First publication of average weekly hours and average hourly earnings (replacing gross payroll aggregates); federal civil service employment reporting begins; sample reaches 70,000 establishments.
- **1935:** **First benchmark** to the biennial Census of Manufactures (a ~12% revision, republishing 1923–1929). Congress passes the **Social Security Act**, creating the unemployment insurance (UI) system — employers' mandatory quarterly UI wage reports become, five years later, the census-like **benchmark source** for CES (via QCEW), a role they still play today.
- **1936:** First national estimate of total nonfarm wage and salary employment.
- **1949:** All states signed cooperative agreements (all 50 states + D.C., PR, VI by 1980).
- **Post-war evolution:** the program has been repeatedly shaped by presidential commissions, statistical-association panels (notably the Gordon Committee in the early 1960s), conversion to probability sampling, the shift from SIC to **NAICS** industry codes (early 2000s), adoption of **concurrent seasonal adjustment**, and the ongoing shift to **electronic/automated data collection** (today mostly web-based and other electronic modes).

This history matters for the dataset's provenance: **industry classifications, series definitions, and benchmark sources have changed repeatedly over 110 years**, so long-horizon time series work requires attention to historical breaks and discontinued series.

## 5. Scope, Sample, & Methodology (What the Data Actually Are)

**Reference period:** the pay period that includes the **12th of the month**.

**Sample and frame:**
- A **stratified, simple random sample of worksites** (clustered by UI account number), drawn from the BLS **Longitudinal Database (LDB)** built from QCEW records — a frame of roughly **12.1 million UI-covered establishments** covering nearly the entire U.S. economy.
- Current sample: approximately **119,000 businesses and government agencies representing ~622,000–629,000 individual worksites** — about **one-third of all nonfarm payroll jobs** (≈26% of all nonfarm payroll employees in the 50 states + D.C.). Strata are defined by state, industry, and employment size; sampling rates set by optimum allocation to minimize error on total nonfarm employment, which is the design's top priority.

**Data collected:** all employees; women employees; production employees (goods-producing) / nonsupervisory employees (private services); total payrolls, commissions, and paid hours (including overtime and paid leave); overtime hours (manufacturing only). All from employer **payroll records**, not worker self-reports.

**Data types produced:** employment (levels, over-the-month changes), average weekly hours, average hourly earnings, average weekly earnings/overtime, diffusion indexes, and related series — published at NAICS detail from supersector down to 3–6-digit industry levels.

**Estimation:**
- **All-employee (AE) series:** weighted-link-relative estimator applied to a **matched sample** (units reporting in both current and prior month), plus a **net business birth–death model** to account for employment change from firm openings/closings not captured in real time by the sample.
- **Other series:** weighted-difference-link-and-taper estimator.
- Outlier/atypical treatment for strikes, disasters, and establishment-specific anomalies.
- **Seasonal adjustment:** concurrent methodology (seasonal factors re-estimated every month using data through the current month).

**Benchmarking (critical to understanding this dataset):** Each year, March employment levels are realigned to **universe counts from QCEW** (UI tax records, plus a small amount of non-UI-covered employment such as railroads and religious organizations). The annual **benchmark revision** is published each February with the January Employment Situation, revising up to five years of seasonally adjusted data. Over the past decade, absolute benchmark revisions have averaged **~0.2%** of total employment.

**Release cycle and revision ladder:** First preliminary estimates are released ~3 weeks after the reference week (in **The Employment Situation**, typically the first Friday of the following month, together with the household survey); each month is then revised twice more before being frozen until annual benchmarking. Real Earnings (inflation-adjusted) and a monthly Strike Report are companion releases.

## 6. Typical Users & Uses

Per BLS, the OMB ICR, and the research literature, CES is arguably the single most closely watched U.S. economic statistic:

- **Monetary policy:** The Federal Reserve and financial markets treat the monthly payroll number (total nonfarm employment change, average hourly earnings) as the marquee indicator in the Employment Situation; it directly moves markets and rate expectations. The Fed's Industrial Production index uses CES data.
- **Macro accounts:** CES is a critical input to **GDP** (Bureau of Economic Analysis), **Productivity and Costs** (BLS), and industrial production.
- **Business cycle dating:** The **NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee** uses CES payroll employment as a core input in declaring recessions and expansions.
- **Federal, state, and local government:** labor-market monitoring, program administration, economic development, revenue forecasting; state and metro CES series underpin much state labor market information (LMI) work.
- **Private sector and organized labor:** compensation benchmarking, contract escalation and wage analysis (CES hours and earnings series are widely used in escalation agreements), site selection, industry analysis.
- **Media and the general public:** the monthly jobs report is a staple of economic journalism; BLS explicitly serves audiences from students and jobseekers to investors.
- **Researchers:** economists, labor economists, and data scientists use CES for high-frequency labor market analysis; NBER and Federal Reserve Board researchers actively study CES methodology itself.

## 7. Benefits to the Public

- **Timeliness:** among the timeliest PFEIs — comprehensive industry detail ~3 weeks after the reference period, every month, for over a century.
- **Comprehensiveness and objectivity:** based on administrative payroll records (hard data on jobs actually paid) rather than household self-reporting; covers ~one-third of all payroll employment directly and is benchmarked annually to near-universe UI records.
- **Free and unrestricted:** all data are public domain (17 U.S.C. § 105 — no copyright on U.S. government works), downloadable in bulk, with a public API.
- **Statistical infrastructure:** CES feeds GDP, productivity, industrial production, and recession dating — the public goods of the national accounts rest partly on it.
- **Democratic accountability:** comparable monthly employment data by industry for every state and metro area lets citizens, journalists, and advocates evaluate economic conditions and policy outcomes locally.
- **Historical value:** an unbroken (though methodologically evolving) monthly record of American employment, hours, and earnings since 1915 — an irreplaceable longitudinal asset.

## 8. Data Access — A Guide for Librarians, Preservationists, and Data Scientists

**Program pages:**
- CES-National: https://www.bls.gov/ces/
- CES-State & Metro: https://www.bls.gov/sae/
- Data gateway: https://www.bls.gov/ces/data/

**Access channels (all free):**
1. **News releases:** *The Employment Situation* (monthly; CES data are the "B tables," household survey data are the "A tables"); *Real Earnings*; annual preliminary and final benchmark releases; the monthly Strike Report. Archived releases available.
2. **Interactive tools:** Series Report (data.bls.gov/series-report), One-Screen/Multi-Screen Data Search, Top Picks, Data Finder — output as HTML or Excel (.xlsx).
3. **BLS Public Data API** (developers.bls.gov) — RESTful JSON access, with v2 supporting longer queries; CES series IDs (e.g., the famous `CES0000000001`, total nonfarm employment, and `CES0500000003`, average hourly earnings) are stable, documented identifiers.
4. **Flat text files:** download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/ce/ — the entire CES time-series database and its metadata (series, mapping, and period files), plus analogous files for state/area (`sm`/`ce` trees). The authoritative bulk channel.
5. **Historical "B" tables** (Employment Situation), archived *Employment and Earnings* print-equivalent tables (2011 forward online; earlier issues at **federal depository libraries** — a key preservation resource).
6. **Vintage data:** BLS maintains an annually updated repository of **published employment values as initially released and all subsequent revisions** (Excel/CSV, 3-digit NAICS and above) — essential for real-time-data (nowcasting) research; for older vintages, researchers use the **Federal Reserve's ALFRED** archive and **FRASER** (St. Louis Fed) for the historical *Employment and Earnings* publication.

**Metadata & documentation:**
- *BLS Handbook of Methods*, CES chapter (with dated archives of prior versions — good provenance practice).
- Technical Notes for the CES Survey and for national benchmarks (bls.gov/web/empsit/cestn.htm; cesbmk.htm).
- CES Published Series list, CES Data Access Tips, FAQs.

**Preservation-relevant notes:**
- Series IDs persist, but **series are discontinued** when industries are redefined (SIC→NAICS, benchmark re-definitions); BLS maintains a "Discontinued Data" section.
- The full revision history (not just latest values) is documented via vintage tables, benchmark articles (with archives back decades), and errata pages.
- Because BLS's LABSTAT database holds only the latest published statistics, **third-party archives (ALFRED/FRASER, ICPSR, depository libraries) are the redundancy layer** for as-first-published values.
- Data gaps exist at specific points (e.g., during government shutdowns when collection/publication lapses).

## 9. Known Limitations, Controversies, & Policy-Relevant Critiques

A policy activist, journalist, or careful data scientist should know:

- **Sampling error and revision:** CES is a sample survey; monthly payroll change estimates carry standard errors (roughly ±60–70k on total nonfarm over-the-month change in recent years), and figures are revised twice before benchmarking.
- **The birth–death model** — used to estimate net employment change from business openings/closings between benchmarks — is the most criticized methodological component, particularly around turning points (it can lag in recessions). It is transparently documented, with residual and forecast components.
- **The 2025 benchmark controversy:** the March 2024 benchmark (published February 2025) revised payroll employment down by **−818,000 (−0.5%)** — the largest downward revision since 2009 — generating substantial public and congressional debate. The March 2025 preliminary benchmark (announced September 2025) came in at **−911,000 (−0.6%)**, with the final revision (published February 2026 with the January 2026 Employment Situation) at **−862,000 (−0.5%) not seasonally adjusted** (−898,000 SA), partly affected by a data reconstruction in the banking series (NAICS 521/522). For context: 10-year average absolute benchmark revisions are ~0.2%, and a recent NBER working paper (Decker, w34924) argues CES revisions remain small relative to, e.g., GDP revisions — but the episode intensified scrutiny of the program.
- **Declining survey response rates** — a society-wide problem for federal surveys — have increased the sample's reliance on imputation and the birth–death model and are widely cited as a driver of larger revisions.
- **Coverage definitions:** "nonfarm payroll employment" excludes agriculture, private households, self-employment, and unpaid family workers (differences from the household survey/CPS are well documented in BLS's "Comparing Employment from BLS Household and Payroll Surveys").
- **Counting jobs, not people:** multiple jobholders are counted multiple times; hours/earnings series cover production and nonsupervisory workers for most detail.

## 10. Related Datasets & Crosswalks

For any CES research project, the companion datasets to know are: **CPS** (household survey — unemployment rate, labor force, alternative measures), **QCEW** (the benchmark universe; county-level employment and wages), **LAUS** (model-based state/local unemployment rates), **JOLTS** (openings and turnover), **BDM** (firm birth/death gross flows), and private-sector comparisons (**ADP** payroll data, used in Fed research on alternative measurement). Federal employment statistics more broadly were reviewed by the **Commission on Evidence-Based Policymaking** and, more recently, proposals to consolidate statistical agencies have made CES's institutional home a live policy question.

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence:**

CES is a designated Principal Federal Economic Indicator and is required for implementation of federal programs (BEA's GDP, the Fed's Industrial Production, BLS productivity). The FY2026 budget justification reaffirms CES among programs "required by statute" and "PFEIs" that will be protected (https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/general/budget/2026/CBJ-2026-V3-01.pdf).
- *High Risk level (counter-argument):* QCEW (UI wage records) is a near-universe employment count that could partially substitute, and ADP provides private payroll estimates. However, QCEW is quarterly with a 5–6 month lag and contains no hours or earnings; no substitute exists for monthly payroll hours/earnings (https://www.bls.gov/sae/questions-and-answers.htm).

**Selected level: No Known Issue.** CES has one of the strongest statutory foundations of any federal dataset: an explicit, century-old monthly publication mandate that names the exact data elements. Partial substitutes exist for employment levels only, with severe timeliness and content limitations.

The FY2026 request cut ~8% of budget (below the 10% Moderate threshold): $703.95M → $647.95M, and −168 FTEs (https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/general/budget/2026/CBJ-2026-V3-01.pdf; https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-06-04/trump-budget-calls-for-bls-cuts-raising-data-quality-concerns).
- *High Risk level:* **Leadership removed** — President Trump fired Senate-confirmed Commissioner Erika McEntarfer on August 1, 2025, hours after a weak jobs report, asserting without evidence the data was "rigged" (https://apnews.com/article/trump-jobs-firing-f00e9bf96d0110519be9bf4f3ec89195; https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/trump-administration/trump-names-brett-matsumoto-bureau-labor-statistics-commissioner-rcna256791). Thirteen of 35 BLS leadership roles sat vacant under a prolonged hiring freeze (https://news.bloomberglaw.com/daily-labor-report/trumps-bls-pick-to-contend-with-leadership-vacuum-staff-losses). Real purchasing power down 14.2% since FY2009. Note: the USAJobs tracker (usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com) was archived December 31, 2025 and tracks job postings rather than headcount, so it cannot corroborate current BLS levels.

**Selected level: High Risk.** The "leadership removed" trigger is squarely met (commissioner fired by presidential action; large fraction of senior roles vacant), compounded by a ~20% staff loss and a proposed 8% budget cut on top of a decade of real decline. A partial mitigant: career economist Brett Matsumoto was confirmed as commissioner on August 7, 2026 and has publicly pledged methodological integrity (Reuters, Aug 7, 2026).

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence:**
- *No Known Issue level:* No evidence of politically driven alteration of CES numbers themselves; no evidence of manipulation has been found despite intense scrutiny; the new commissioner states method changes "will be approved by career staff... and communicated to the public ahead of time" (Reuters, Aug 7, 2026).
- *Moderate Risk level:* The FY2026 budget **proposes reorganizing BLS, BEA, and Census into the Department of Commerce** — a pending structural change whose details "are still to be shared" (https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/general/budget/2026/CBJ-2026-V3-01.pdf; ASA report). This would relocate the dataset's institutional home.
- *High Risk level:* Sustained presidential-level attacks on CES-derived data: Trump called the jobs numbers "rigged," fired the commissioner over them, and initially nominated E.J. Antoni — an outspoken BLS critic — before withdrawing the nomination (NBC News; Reuters). BLS's technical and data-user advisory committees and FESAC were disbanded by the Administration (ASA report; Reuters). The Administration's budget language refocusing BLS on PFEIs "in accordance with Administration priorities" has already driven product eliminations agency-wide (e.g., state JOLTS cut from monthly to annual), demonstrating that policy-driven narrowing extends to employment data products (https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2026/08/statistical-agency-staffing-cuts-federal-data-scrutiny/415399/; House Ed & Labor Democrats' letter).

**Selected level: High Risk.** The commissioner's firing over CES data, the nomination of a critic, the disbanding of advisory committees, and the pending forced reorganization of BLS into Commerce constitute significant Administration-driven changes to the program's environment, even though the series' content has not been demonstrably politicized. Confirmation of a career-economist commissioner in August 2026 is a genuine but partial de-escalation.

---

## Summary of Risk Levels

| Category | Level |
|---|---|
| **Historical Data Availability** | **Moderate Risk** — ~900 state/area series removed from the database with the January 2026 benchmark; national history intact |
| **Future Data Availability** | **High Risk** — October 2025 monthly publication skipped and statutory monthly cadence missed; repeated shutdown-driven delays; ICR active through 8/31/2027 and currently on schedule |
| **Data Quality** | **High Risk** — granularity and timeliness already reduced; record-large benchmark revisions; declining sample coverage and response rates |
| **Statutory Context** | **No Known Issue** — explicit monthly statutory mandate (29 U.S.C. § 2), PFEI status, required for GDP and other federal programs; no adequate substitute |
| **Staffing and Funding** | **High Risk** — commissioner fired by presidential action; ~20% staff loss since FY2024; 13/35 leadership roles vacant; proposed 8% budget cut and forced reorganization |
| **Policy** | **High Risk** — presidential attacks on the data, leadership purge, advisory committees disbanded, pending relocation of BLS to Commerce; partially mitigated by the new commissioner's integrity commitments |

**Overall judgment:** The single most important protection this dataset has is its statute — Congress has required monthly publication of exactly these statistics since 1930, and no administration has proposed terminating CES, which is among the most protected (PFEI) of BLS programs. The realistic near-term risks are not elimination but **degradation**: continued shutdown-driven gaps in the monthly cadence, further series discontinuations as sample coverage erodes, larger revisions, and a disruptive relocation of the program to the Commerce Department if the reorganization proposal advances. Preservationists should prioritize archiving the ~900 discontinued state/area series histories, vintage (as-first-published) values, and the flat-file snapshots, since BLS's live database only holds latest-published values.
